html:
Madhava's infinite series are formulas for pi and for the sine, cosine and arctangent found by Madhava of Sangamagrama, a mathematician in Kerala who lived around 1340 to 1425.

An infinite series writes a number as an endless sum of ever smaller terms. Madhava showed, for example, that pi divided by four equals 1 minus a third plus a fifth minus a seventh, and so on forever. He also found ways to correct the sum when it is cut off, and used them to work out pi to eleven decimal places.

These results came about 250 years before Gregory, Leibniz and Newton found the same series in Europe. They are a key early step toward calculus.

Almost none of Madhava's own writing survives. We know his work through the Kerala school that followed him, above all Nilakantha's Tantrasangraha of 1501 and the Yuktibhasa of about 1530, which gives proofs. The school built on the tradition of Aryabhata. Whether its ideas ever reached Europe is still argued.
sum: Madhava's infinite series are formulas for pi and for the sine, cosine and arctangent found by Madhava of Sangamagrama, a mathematician in Kerala who lived around 1340 to 1425.
